section.title: How Long, O Lord
section.sectionRationale: One of the shortest and most tightly patterned laments in the Psalter, moving in six verses from a fourfold cry of 'how long' through urgent petition to a resolved vow of trust and song. It is a model of how honest complaint and settled faith can live in the very same prayer, and it stands early in Book I among David's psalms of personal distress.
section.thesis: David's raw, repeated 'how long' does not stay in despair; brought honestly before God it turns, without any change in circumstance, into trust in His loving devotion and a resolve to sing.
section.frameNote: Three short movements: the fourfold complaint, how long; the urgent petition, consider and answer me; and the turn to trust, I have trusted, I will sing.

verses.text:
How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? 
How long will You hide Your face from me?

How long must I wrestle in my {{nephesh|soul}}, with sorrow in my heart each day? 
How long will my enemy dominate me?
Consider me and respond, O LORD my God. Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death,
lest my enemy say, “I have overcome him,” and my foes rejoice when I fall.

units.label: I will sing to the Lord

verses.text: But I have trusted in Your {{chesed|loving devotion}}; my heart will rejoice in Your {{yeshuah|salvation}}.
I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me.

nephesh.gloss: Soul, inner self, the whole living person including mind and emotion, not merely a detached spirit. David wrestles in his nephesh, meaning the sorrow has settled into the very core of who he is, not just his outward circumstances.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast, covenant loving devotion, God's loyal love bound to His promises. It is the anchor David reaches for when nothing in his circumstances has changed; the feeling has not lifted, but the chesed he trusts in has not moved.

yeshuah.gloss: Salvation, deliverance, rescue. The same root behind the name Jesus, Yeshua, He saves. David's rejoicing in God's yeshuah before any rescue has arrived anticipates the fuller salvation later revealed and named in Christ.

basic.context: David feels forgotten and hidden from, worn down by sorrow every day, and pressed by an enemy who seems to be winning. He does not hide this from God; he brings it to Him directly, four times crying 'how long'. Then, still without any change in his circumstances, he asks God to look at him, to answer, to give him life. By the last two verses something has shifted inside him: he says he has trusted, and he resolves to sing.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real prayer of lament, meant to be prayed, not merely studied. It gives permission and a pattern for honest complaint to God, and it shows that biblical faith does not require pretending things are fine; it requires bringing the real ache to the true God and choosing, even in the ache, to trust Him.
basic.originalLanguages: David wrestles in his nephesh, his whole inner self, not merely at the surface. What steadies him is not new information but chesed, God's steadfast covenant love, unchanged by David's feelings. His hope is called yeshuah, salvation, the very word behind the name of Jesus, He saves.
basic.typology: David's pattern of honest lament turning to trust anticipates the greater sufferer, Christ, who also cried out in anguish, 'My God, my God, why have You forsaken me', and who, like David here, entrusted Himself finally to the Father who saves.
basic.christ: Jesus prayed His own 'how long' from the cross, quoting a psalm just a few pages later, Psalm 22. He shows us that crying out to God in raw distress is not unbelief; it is the shape faith takes under real suffering, a faith that, like David's, still ends in trust and praise.
basic.god: God is not offended by David's repeated 'how long'. He is the kind of God who can be pressed, questioned, and pleaded with, and who is trusted precisely because His loving devotion, His chesed, does not depend on how quickly He answers.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 22:1-2 voices the same 'how long' cry, later prayed by Christ on the cross. Romans 8:24-25 speaks of a hope that waits patiently for what is not yet seen. Lamentations 3:19-24 moves through the same pattern, from anguish to remembered steadfast love.
basic.oneStory: David's short prayer shows the whole Bible's pattern in miniature: honest cries in a broken world met by the steadfast love of God, a love fully proven in Christ, who endured His own greater 'how long' so that our songs of trust would have a sure and final foundation.

context.literary:
The four questions of verses 1 and 2 are not a jumble. They run through the three parties of a lament: God (forget, hide), the speaker himself (counsels in the soul, sorrow in the heart), and the enemy (rising over me). Older studies of the psalms noticed this triangle of You, I and they, and it is worth watching how each question drags the pain a little closer to home, from what God is doing, to what David is doing, to what his enemy is doing.

The psalm also has a quiet progress in how it names God. In verse 1 he is simply 'O LORD', the covenant name, spoken into what feels like silence. In verse 3 the address grows into 'O LORD my God', a possessive that David reaches for exactly when God seems least his. The complaint speaks of God in the second person, and the petition asks three things in a run, look, answer, light, each urgent and short, followed by two 'lest' clauses that name the fear behind the asking: death, and the enemy's boast.

Then comes a hinge in a single word, 'But', with the pronoun placed first for emphasis, so that it reads something like 'But as for me'. Everything before it is what David feels; what follows is what David does. The two verbs of verse 5 and the final verb of verse 6 refer to things done and things resolved, and the psalm closes with a reason that looks backward: 'He has been good to me.' The past tense matters. David is not celebrating a rescue that has just arrived. He is remembering earlier kindness, and letting it outweigh the present silence.

Coming after Psalm 12, which speaks of the pure words of the LORD against the lying tongues of the proud, this psalm gives the personal side of the same struggle, and Psalm 14 turns at once to the fool who says there is no God.
context.historical:
The title reads 'For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.' Two things follow from that. First, the psalm was handed over to the temple musicians, so a prayer that began as one man's private ache was meant to be sung aloud by the congregation. Israel did not treat honest complaint as something to hide in the dark; she put it in the songbook, and the assembled worshipers learned to pray the 'how long' of others long before they needed to pray it themselves. Second, the title supplies an author but no occasion, and the psalm itself names none.

Readers have often thought of the long years when Saul hunted David, since the story tells of a spear thrown at him twice in the house, 1 Samuel 18:10-11, and of David as a man who could do nothing to speed his rescue. Others think of the time of Absalom's revolt. The text does not choose between these, and the lack of a named event is part of its usefulness: any generation of sufferers can step into the words.

The fear of 'sleeping in death' has to be heard in an Israelite ear. In the Old Testament, death was a place of silence in which the worshiper is cut off from the assembly and its praise, as Psalm 6:5 puts it, 'For there is no mention of You in death; who can praise You from Sheol?' To die at the enemy's hand was therefore not only the end of life but the end of testimony, and worse, it would seem to hand the enemy a verdict. In a world where the outcome of a struggle was read as a judgement on the parties, the enemy's cry 'I have overcome him' would sound as if God had been beaten as well. That is why the petition of verse 4 pleads for God's own honour as well as David's safety.
context.canonical:
Psalm 13 belongs to a large family of 'how long' prayers scattered through the Psalter and beyond: Psalm 6:3, Psalm 35:17, Psalm 74:10, Psalm 79:5, Psalm 89:46, Psalm 90:13 and Psalm 94:3. The prophets take up the same language. Habakkuk begins, 'How long, O LORD, must I call for help but You do not hear,' Habakkuk 1:2. The cry is picked up in the last book of the Bible by the martyrs under the altar, who ask, 'How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood,' Revelation 6:10. In all of these the question is asked of God, never against Him, and never as a substitute for trust.

The Bible also answers the question in more than one way. Sometimes God answers by acting, as in Psalm 22:22-24, where the sufferer learns that the LORD 'has not hidden His face from him, but has attended to his cry for help.' Sometimes He answers by asking for patience, as in the word to Habakkuk that the vision 'lingers' but 'will surely come and will not delay,' Habakkuk 2:3. And in the story of the unjust judge Jesus says that God will 'promptly carry out justice' for His elect who cry out day and night, Luke 18:7-8, while asking whether the Son of Man will find faith when He comes.

The psalm's pattern of complaint, petition and settled trust returns in Lamentations 3:19-24, where the poet passes from 'Remember my affliction' to 'Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope.' The 'But I' of Psalm 13:5 is the same turn. The New Testament supplies the ground of it: Paul says hope that is seen is no hope at all, and that those who hope for what they do not yet see 'wait for it patiently,' Romans 8:24-25.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David, and the choirmaster who received his psalm, meant to give a whole congregation a way to pray when God seems to have gone quiet. The first hearers were not to leave the psalm thinking that faith means feeling secure. They were meant to learn that a person can say four times, 'How long?', and still be speaking to the God who has not left. The structure teaches by its order: the complaint is allowed its full length before any comfort arrives, and the comfort, when it comes, is not an argument but a decision to remember what God has been.

The psalm is also careful about what it asks. David does not ask that his enemy be destroyed. He asks God to look, to answer, and to keep him alive, and he ties that request to a fear about God's reputation, that his foes will say they have won. To the first hearers this meant that a suffering believer should bring the heart, the body and the good name of God together into prayer. They were meant to walk away willing to wait, sure that the God who is addressed as 'my God' in the darkest verse is the God who will be praised in the last.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes David's feelings and does not command anyone to feel them. It does not tell readers to expect God to hide His face, and it does not claim that every experience of silence means God is displeased. What is prescribed is the movement: bring the complaint to God by name, ask for specific things, and let trust have the last word, even when nothing outside has changed.

This matters for how the psalm is used. It can be prayed by someone in depression, in prolonged illness, in an unjust dispute or in a long wait for an answer, and it can be prayed on behalf of others, as the church has prayed it for the persecuted. It should not be turned into a formula that guarantees a swift ending, since the psalm itself leaves David's circumstances exactly where they were. Nor should the last two verses be used to hurry a sufferer past the first four. The order of the psalm is a pastoral instruction: the sorrow is spoken first and in full, and the singing follows in its own time.

debates.question: Does the shift to trust in verses 5 and 6 mean David's circumstances had already changed?

views.label: Nothing in the text changes; the shift is internal, an act of will and faith
views.case: No deliverance is narrated between verse 4 and verse 5; the turn happens through prayer itself, showing that trust can precede rescue. The verbs of verse 5 speak of trusting and rejoicing, and of what David resolves to do, not of an event.

views.label: Some form of assurance, perhaps a word from a priest or an inward conviction, prompted the change
views.case: Similar shifts elsewhere in the Psalter, for example Psalm 6:8-9, where the speaker says the LORD has heard his weeping, may reflect an assurance received in worship, though the text does not say so explicitly here.

debates.bearing: Either reading affirms that the turn to trust is genuine and given by God; the psalm still teaches that faith can rest in God's character before it sees His deliverance, and that the honest cry belongs in worship.

debates.question: Who is the 'enemy' of verses 2 and 4?

views.label: A human adversary, most naturally a political or personal rival
views.case: The enemy 'dominates' David and waits to say 'I have overcome him', and his 'foes' rejoice at David's fall, verse 4. That reads most naturally as people, and the setting of a king pursued by rivals, as in the years of Saul, fits it.

views.label: Sickness or death, or the people who read his sickness as a sign of guilt
views.case: The fear of 'sleeping in death' and of eyes that need light has led some to read the psalm as the prayer of a sick person. On that view the enemy is the illness and those who gloat over it. Psalm 38:15-16, where mockers wait for a slipping foot, shows how suffering and mockery are joined in the Psalter.

views.label: An open-ended figure, so that any hostile power can be prayed against
views.case: The lack of names lets the psalm serve for spiritual opposition as well. Christian readers have often prayed it against the enemy of souls, since the New Testament speaks of the powers disarmed at the cross, Colossians 2:15.

debates.bearing: The psalm does not settle the question, and its usefulness lies in that. All three readings agree on what David asks: not vengeance, but that God will look, answer, and not let the enemy boast.

study.originalLanguages:
The four 'how long' questions each begin with the Hebrew phrase ad anah, literally 'until where?' or 'to what point?' It is not a request for information about time but a protest at the length of the delay, Other 'how long' prayers, such as Psalm 6:3 and Psalm 74:10, use a near synonym, ad matai, 'until when.' In verse 1 the first question is joined to a word for 'forever'; the fear is not only that God is late but that the silence might have no end.

In verse 2 the BSB says 'wrestle in my soul.' The Hebrew, as I read it, says something more like 'How long shall I set counsels in my soul?' The noun is the plural of a word for plans or advice, and the picture is of a man laying plan after plan in his inner self, sorting through options, arguing with himself, with no rest for the deliberation. The English 'wrestle' catches the effect but hides the picture. It is the anxiety of someone with no counsel to lean on but his own.

The petition of verse 3, 'Give light to my eyes,' uses a causative form of the verb 'to be light.' The same verb appears when Jonathan tastes honey and 'his eyes brightened,' 1 Samuel 14:27, when Ezra says God has given 'light to our eyes,' Ezra 9:8, and when the commandments are 'radiant, giving light to the eyes,' Psalm 19:8. Bright eyes are the mark of vitality, and dull eyes the mark of a life running out. David is asking to be revived, and the 'lest I sleep in death' that follows is the darker side of the same picture.

In verse 5 the two halves of the line differ in kind. 'I have trusted' looks at something already settled, while 'my heart will rejoice' looks ahead to what has not yet happened. The trust is done and the rejoicing waits, and the word 'salvation' in the second half is the family of words that gives Jesus His name.

The last word of the psalm turns on gamal, the verb behind 'has been good to me.' It means to deal fully with someone, to render to them what a long course of action has earned or merited, and it can be used of good or of evil. Psalm 116:7 uses it in a passage that looks like a companion piece: 'Return to your rest, O my soul, for the LORD has been good to you.' David closes by counting what the LORD has already rendered him. Finally, verse 4's 'when I fall' uses the verb mot, the same root that Psalm 15:5 and Psalm 16:8 use for being shaken, so that the enemy's hope in Psalm 13 is exactly what the next psalms deny.

typology.type: David's 'how long' cried out in faith
typology.fulfillment: The cry of a suffering king who is forgotten and hidden from takes its fullest form in Christ. From the cross He prayed the first words of Psalm 22, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?', Matthew 27:46, and the Letter to the Hebrews speaks of the days when He offered up prayers 'with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death,' Hebrews 5:7. David's silence lasted for a season; Christ entered the deepest silence there is. The type falls short because David was never truly abandoned on account of sin, while Christ bore the weight of it in our place, 2 Corinthians 5:21.

typology.type: 'Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death'
typology.fulfillment: David asks to be kept from the sleep of death. Scripture regularly calls death a sleep for those who die in the Lord, and it says Christ has been raised, 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20. The plea for light to the eyes is answered in Him, and Paul can borrow the language: 'Wake up, O sleeper, rise up from the dead, and Christ will shine on you,' Ephesians 5:14. The pattern is real but partial, since David asks only to be spared death for a while, while Christ passes through death and out the other side, so that His people can face it without fear.

typology.type: The enemy who says, 'I have overcome him'
typology.fulfillment: David fears that his foe will crow over him. At the cross the mockers said, 'He saved others, but He cannot save Himself,' Matthew 27:42, and it looked as though the enemy had won. The resurrection reverses the boast: God 'disarmed the powers and authorities' and triumphed over them by the cross, Colossians 2:15. The correspondence is that the same shape of humiliation and reversal is at work; the escalation is that Christ's victory is universal and final, so that Paul can taunt death itself, 1 Corinthians 15:55-57. David's own foes were only a foreshadowing.

typology.type: The heart that rejoices in salvation
typology.fulfillment: David resolves to rejoice in God's yeshuah, the word from the family behind the name Jesus. When Simeon takes the infant Christ in his arms he says, 'For my eyes have seen Your salvation,' Luke 2:30, and Matthew records that the child is to be named Jesus 'because He will save His people from their sins,' Matthew 1:21. What David hoped to see, Simeon holds. The type is an anticipation; the salvation David sings of is a rescue from enemies, while the salvation Christ brings reaches to sin and death.

study.christ:
It is worth saying plainly that Psalm 13 is not quoted in the New Testament, and the Gospels do not treat it as a direct prophecy of Christ. Its way to Him is by pattern and by theme. It shows the shape of a righteous sufferer's prayer, and Christ prays that shape more fully than anyone.

By pattern, the four 'how long' questions sit close to the psalm that Christ took on His lips, Psalm 22. The one who cried, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?', Matthew 27:46, did not invent a new form of prayer; He took the Psalter's own language of complaint, and the Letter to the Hebrews says His prayers were offered 'with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverence,' Hebrews 5:7. Psalm 22 moves the way Psalm 13 moves, from 'Why are You so far from saving me' to 'You who fear the LORD, praise Him,' Psalm 22:1, 22-23, and the last words of Christ on the cross, 'Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit,' Luke 23:46, are taken from Psalm 31:5, a psalm of trust in which the sufferer commits himself to the LORD. So the arc of honest lament into trust is not merely David's; it is walked through by the Son.

By theme, Psalm 13 feels the threat of the enemy's boast, 'I have overcome him,' and the rescue of the psalm's 'eyes' and 'sleep of death.' Christ meets both. On the cross the chief priests said, 'He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him,' Matthew 27:43, in effect the very sneer David dreaded. The resurrection is God's answer to it: He 'disarmed the powers and authorities,' Colossians 2:15, and made Christ 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20. The 'sleep in death' from which David asked to be spared is the sleep Christ passed through and left behind.

By name, David's word for what he hopes in, 'salvation', is in the same family as the name Jesus, given to Him 'because He will save His people from their sins,' Matthew 1:21.

There is also a comfort here for the person praying the psalm. We do not have a high priest 'who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses,' but one 'who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin,' Hebrews 4:15, and so we are invited to 'approach the throne of grace with confidence,' Hebrews 4:16. The believer who prays 'how long' is praying with the one who has already prayed it, and who has been heard.

A caution is needed. Christ's cry from the cross was of a different order from David's. David asks not to be forgotten and his enemy will not triumph; Christ bears the abandonment the psalm can only fear, so that His people never will. It would be wrong to read every phrase of Psalm 13 as spoken by Jesus, and this study does not.
study.god:
Psalm 13 gives us a God who can be pressed. The four questions of the opening are not rebuked, and the psalm sits in the songbook that Israel was to sing in the presence of the LORD. The book that God Himself gave His people includes prayers that accuse Him of forgetting, and He allowed them to be kept. That tells us something about His character: He is secure enough in His goodness to be questioned, and kind enough to receive the complaint as prayer.

The psalm holds together two things that seem in conflict. God is the one who, on David's account, hides His face and seems to forget. Yet He is also 'the LORD my God' and the one to whom the whole psalm is addressed. Scripture is willing to say both. The hiding of the face can be a judgement, as in Deuteronomy 31:17-18, where God warns that He will hide His face from a people who turn to other gods; but it can also be brief and gracious, as in Isaiah 54:7-8, 'For a brief moment I forsook you, but with great compassion I will bring you back.' Psalm 13 does not tell us which kind of hiding David is enduring, and it does not need to. What it insists on is that the hidden God is still the God to whom one may speak.

God's goodness is shown as a settled fact rather than a passing mood. David's last word is that the LORD 'has been good to me', a reference to what God has already done. God does not have to prove Himself anew each morning for His people to be sure of Him. When Zion says, 'The LORD has forsaken me; the Lord has forgotten me!', He answers, 'Can a woman forget her nursing child ... Even if she could forget, I will not forget you!' Isaiah 49:14-15. The feeling of being forgotten and the fact of being forgotten are not the same.

His loving devotion, the covenant chesed of verse 5, is the ground of trust: it does not rise and fall with David's feelings or with the pace of the answer. Lamentations 3:22-23 says the same: 'Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail.'

He is also the God who keeps time in His own way. Habakkuk is told to wait for a vision that 'lingers' yet 'will surely come and will not delay,' Habakkuk 2:3, and Jesus says God will 'promptly carry out justice' for those who cry to Him day and night, Luke 18:7-8. The two statements are held together: the delay is real to the sufferer, and it is not neglect.

For worship, the psalm teaches us to sing what we do not yet feel. The last two verses are a decision of the will, made with open eyes: 'I will sing to the LORD.' A congregation that has learned Psalm 13 can worship with its sorrow rather than in spite of it, and can stand beside the person who cannot yet sing.

crossReferences.note: Another prayer that asks 'How long, O LORD, how long?' and grounds the plea in the fear of death: 'For there is no mention of You in death; who can praise You from Sheol?' It explains why David dreads sleeping in death in Psalm 13:3, since to die is to lose the assembly and its praise.

The psalm Christ prayed from the cross, Matthew 27:46. It shares Psalm 13's sense of being far from help and unanswered day and night, but it is the fuller lament, reaching a public song of praise in verses 22 to 24.

The nation's version of David's complaint: 'Why do You hide Your face and forget our affliction and oppression?' The same two verbs, hide and forget, appear in Psalm 13:1, showing that the personal lament and the communal lament use one vocabulary.

Another 'How long, O LORD?' set beside the question 'Will You hide Yourself forever?' It shows that even a psalm whose foundation is the promise to David can end in a plea, and that the covenant is not a reason to hush the cry.

A psalm of thanksgiving that reads like the answer to Psalm 13. The same verb as 'has been good to me' appears in 'the LORD has been good to you,' and the sufferer who feared death now says his soul has been delivered from it.

Moves from the memory of affliction to 'Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope,' and then to the LORD as 'my portion.' It carries the same turn as the 'But I' of Psalm 13:5: hope does not deny the sorrow but chooses what to remember beside it.

The prophet's version of the question, 'How long, O LORD, must I call for help but You do not hear.' God's answer in Habakkuk 2:3-4 is not an explanation but a call to wait, and 'the righteous will live by faith.'

Zion says, 'The LORD has forsaken me; the Lord has forgotten me!' and God answers with the picture of a mother who could not forget her child. It gives divine reply to the fear in Psalm 13:1 that God has forgotten.

Jesus asks whether God will not bring about justice for those who cry out to Him day and night, and promises that He will 'promptly carry out justice.' It places every 'how long' prayer under the Lord's assurance, while reminding believers to keep the faith while they wait.

The martyrs under the altar cry, 'How long, O Lord, holy and true,' and are told to rest a little longer. The 'how long' of Psalm 13 is still being prayed at the end of the age, and it is heard, though not yet finally answered.

Paul says 'hope that is seen is no hope at all' and that those who hope for what they do not yet see 'wait for it patiently.' This is the New Testament's account of the position David is in as he says, 'I have trusted.'

study.oneStory:
Psalm 13 sits inside the first great rupture of the story. Since Genesis 3 the world has been a place where, to a believer's eye, God can look absent and evil can look successful. The enemy of verse 4 who says 'I have overcome him' is a small, personal echo of the serpent who said, 'You will not surely die,' and of every voice since that has told a sufferer that God has lost the fight. The psalm comes from the same stretch of the story as the exile from Eden: living east of the garden, with the presence of God no longer to be taken for granted, and prayer as the way back in.

It also answers a question the story keeps raising: what should a person of faith do while a promise is unfulfilled? Abraham waited for the child, Israel for the land, and the exiles for the return. The psalm shows the answer in miniature. Tell God the whole truth, ask Him for what you need, and remember what He has done, and so keep faith in the meantime. The same posture is required at the great turning points, when the prophets call a people to wait for a vision that 'lingers,' Habakkuk 2:3.

The story then supplies what the psalm can only long for. Christ enters the place of abandonment, prays the psalms of complaint from the cross, and is raised, so that the enemy's boast is silenced and death becomes a sleep. His resurrection is 'a living hope' and the seal of 'an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading,' 1 Peter 1:3-4. The believer who prays Psalm 13 prays it from the far side of the empty tomb, and the 'but I have trusted' of verse 5 rests on something David could only look toward.

The story ends with the last 'how long' answered. The martyrs are told to rest a little longer, Revelation 6:10-11, and then the new creation opens: God dwells with His people, and He wipes every tear, Revelation 21:3-4. Nothing will be hidden, nothing forgotten, and the songs the psalmist promised to sing are sung without an enemy in earshot.

quiz.q: What is the pattern of Psalm 13's structure?

options.text: Fourfold complaint, urgent petition, then a resolved turn to trust and song.
options.note: This three part movement, from plea to praise, is the psalm's clear shape.

options.text: A long complaint followed by a description of the enemy's defeat.
options.note: Close, but no defeat of the enemy is narrated; the turn is internal trust, not a reported victory.

options.text: A song of praise interrupted by a brief complaint.
options.note: This reverses the actual order; the complaint comes first and the praise follows.

options.text: A series of unrelated proverbs about patience.
options.note: The psalm is a unified personal lament and prayer, not a collection of proverbs.

quiz.q: What does David ask for in verses 3-4?

options.text: That God would consider him, answer him, and give light to his eyes so he would not sleep in death.
options.note: This is his direct, urgent petition for God's attention and life.

options.text: That God would destroy his enemy immediately.
options.note: David mentions the enemy's gloating as a concern, but his direct request is for God's own attention and life, not the enemy's destruction.

options.text: That God would explain why He has hidden His face.
options.note: Close to his complaint in verses 1-2, but his actual petition in verses 3-4 asks for God's attention and life, not an explanation.

options.text: That his sorrow would simply be forgotten.
options.note: David does not ask to forget his sorrow; he asks God to act and answer him.

quiz.q: What has changed by verses 5-6, and what has not?

options.text: No circumstance is shown to change, yet David's heart moves to trust in God's loving devotion and resolves to sing.
options.note: The text narrates no rescue; the shift is a fresh act of trust and praise.

options.text: David's enemy is explicitly defeated before he sings.
options.note: No defeat of the enemy is narrated in the text.

options.text: David receives a direct audible answer from God before rejoicing.
options.note: No such audible answer is recorded; his trust rests on God's character, not a reported new revelation.

options.text: His sorrow is instantly removed and forgotten.
options.note: His posture changes to trust and song, though this reflects a shift in his heart more than an erasure of the underlying sorrow.

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew word chesed emphasize in verse 5?

options.text: God's steadfast, covenant loving devotion, loyal love bound to His promises rather than to circumstances.
options.note: Chesed is the anchor David reaches for precisely because it does not depend on his feelings or timing.

options.text: A general feeling of niceness or pleasantness.
options.note: Chesed carries far more weight than a vague pleasant feeling; it is covenant loyalty and loving commitment.

options.text: God's raw power to defeat enemies.
options.note: Chesed refers to loving devotion and loyalty, not primarily to displays of power.

options.text: A momentary emotion that quickly fades.
options.note: This misses chesed's core meaning as a steadfast, enduring commitment rather than a passing emotion.

quiz.q: How does this psalm anticipate Christ?

options.text: Jesus later prays a parallel 'how long' cry from the cross, quoting Psalm 22, and models the same pattern of honest anguish resolved in trust toward the Father.
options.note: Christ's own cry of abandonment shows the same honest lament, ultimately entrusted to the Father who saves.

options.text: It predicts the exact day and hour of the crucifixion.
options.note: The psalm gives no such specific prediction; its connection to Christ is in the pattern of lament and trust, not a date.

options.text: It describes David's own future resurrection.
options.note: The psalm is about David's present distress and trust, not a stated hope of his own bodily resurrection.

options.text: It has no meaningful connection to the New Testament.
options.note: This understates the strong pattern connection, especially to Christ's cry of dereliction on the cross.

questions: David cries 'how long' four times without pretending things are fine. Where do you need to bring an honest, unresolved 'how long' to God this week rather than hiding it?
David asks God to 'consider me and respond' before anything has changed. What would it look like for you to pray boldly for God's attention even while your circumstances remain the same?

By the end of the psalm, David trusts and resolves to sing though nothing outward has shifted. Have you ever experienced that kind of inward turn to trust before the answer came? What helped it happen?
Chesed, God's steadfast loving devotion, does not depend on David's feelings. Where are you tempted to measure God's love by your circumstances rather than by His unchanging character?
Jesus prayed His own 'how long' from the cross. How does knowing that Christ entered fully into this kind of honest anguish change the way you bring your own laments to God?

translationNotes.note: The fourfold repetition of 'how long' in the Hebrew intensifies the sense of prolonged, unresolved distress; English translations preserve this by repeating the phrase at the start of each clause.
Loving devotion renders chesed, God's covenant loyal love; some translations render it lovingkindness or steadfast love, all pointing to the same durable, promise-keeping love.
Salvation renders yeshuah, the same root later given as the personal name Jesus, Yeshua, He saves, linking David's hope of rescue to the name of the one who fulfills it.
